newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ SPORT, RUGBY UNION - "We're not mercenaries" says Mehrtens.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT, RUGBY UNION - "We're not mercenaries" says Mehrtens.

text.p: CHRISTCHURCH, Sept 25 - New Zealand rugby players were not mercenaries and few players would change provinces under the transfer player system in November, All Black Andrew Mehrtens said on Wednesday.
He said nothing would stop some players going to Japan, to rugby league or to northern hemisphere club rugby, but most players would stay loyal to their provinces.
"I know I'm not keen to leave Canterbury. I couldn't imagine playing against Canterbury. I would only move for a reason, not for money," he told NZPA.
"I guess there will be some movements but the strength of New Zealand rugby is in the provinces and it's up to them to instill loyalty."
Mehrtens said the national provincial championship (NPC) was showing players were parochial and had pride in their provinces.

"I would still play for Canterbury even if I wasn't being paid. The primary reason for playing is for pride and enjoyment. The reality is you must get fun out of it or if you didn't enjoy it you would do something else."
Mehrtens said it would take a few years for provinces to test the waters of the new system.
Under the scheme, provincial unions could only buy in five players a year and they would have to pay $125,000 to buy a star All Black, compared with $15,000 for a second division NPC player.
New Zealand schoolboy players would cost $10,000, former All Blacks $40,000 and established All Blacks $75,000.
Transfers have to take place in the month of November.
Mehrtens said the system set up by the New Zealand Rugby Football Union was a start in an effort to keep players in their provinces.
Canterbury rugby chief executive Stephen Tew said his union was not wealthy enough to sign up all their current players for next season. But he did not rule out buying in outside players.
Tew said retention of current players was the No 1 priority but the dawning of professional rugby was putting a strain on the union's finances.
"The question everyone will want to know is how much to pay the players," he told NZPA.
But he said there was a balancing act -- Canterbury had to consider the need to buy in key players too.
